hook.text: One user, a hundred thousand items, and an embedding for each. Score every item, and return the ten closest. In NumPy, that's a few lines, and the coding round asks what those lines cost, and where they break.

plan.text: It's a normal data-structures interview, pointed at machine learning. Fifteen questions: ten worked through, then five quick ones.

q1.text: Question one. Why does NumPy vectorization beat a Python for loop?

q1-time.text: Score a hundred thousand items, sixty-four numbers each, against the user. Timed once, in the browser's Python, a plain loop is roughly a hundred times slower than one matrix product, with the same answers.

q1-why.text: The loop runs interpreted bytecode for every multiply. The product is one call into precompiled C, over a contiguous, typed buffer, with SIMD: one instruction on several numbers at once.
q1-why.spoken: The loop runs interpreted bytecode for every multiply. The product is one call into precompiled C, over a contiguous, typed buffer, with sim-dee: one instruction on several numbers at once.

q1-row.text: The follow-up: what about calling NumPy once per row?

q2.text: Question two. How do you compute cosine similarity in NumPy? The dot product, divided by both lengths, so it measures the angle and ignores magnitude. For a catalog, scale every row to length one once, and one matrix product gives every similarity.

q2-zero.text: The guard on the denominator is the one people forget. Say a new item, with no history yet, has an embedding of all zeros. Its similarity is zero over zero: not a number. NumPy sorts that after every real number, so a descending top three puts the empty item first, for every single user.

q2-guard.text: Add a tiny constant to the denominator, and it scores zero instead.

q3.text: Question three. How do you find the top-k scores efficiently? Sorting everything is n log n, and most of that work is wasted. argpartition moves the k largest to one end in linear time, unordered, and then you sort only those k.
q3.spoken: Question three. How do you find the top-k scores efficiently? Sorting everything is n log n, and most of that work is wasted. Arg partition moves the k largest to one end in linear time, unordered, and then you sort only those k.

q3-time.text: On a million scores, timed the same way, that's more than ten times faster than a full sort. In plain Python, or over a stream, keep a heap of size k instead. That's n log k, with memory for only k items.

q4.text: Question four. What is broadcasting, and why is it useful? NumPy stretches the smaller array along its size-one dimensions, without copying. Subtract the column means, a row of two, from a three-by-two matrix, and that row is reused for every row.

q4-trap.text: The trap is that it never complains. Predictions in a column, a thousand by one, minus labels in a flat array of a thousand, broadcast to a thousand by a thousand. The mean squared error comes out two point three instead of point two four, and nothing raises an error. Check the shapes before you reduce.

q5.text: Question five. How do you compute pairwise Euclidean distances between rows? Broadcasting every row against every other gives an n by n by d array. For ten thousand rows of a hundred and twenty-eight numbers in float sixty-four, that's about a hundred gigabytes.

q5-identity.text: Expand the square instead: two squared norms, minus twice the dot product. That's one matrix product, and an n by n result of eight hundred megabytes.

q5-neg.text: The catch is rounding. On a thousand random rows, the squared distance from a row to itself, which should be zero, came out negative for four in ten. The square root turned them into not a number. So clip at zero, before the root.

q6.text: Question six. Why do float thirty-two versus float sixty-four matter for ML data? Float thirty-two halves memory and bandwidth, and it's what GPUs run on. Ten million embeddings of a hundred and twenty-eight numbers take about five gigabytes in float thirty-two, and ten in float sixty-four.

q6-cost.text: The price is precision: about seven significant digits. Add point one to a float thirty-two running total ten million times, and it ends at one million eighty-eight thousand, nine percent high. Near a million, each point one is rounded to an eighth.

q6-fix.text: NumPy's own sum adds in pairs, and misses by only an eighth. So store big arrays in float thirty-two, and keep long running totals in float sixty-four.

q7.text: Question seven. Why subtract the max before exponentiating in softmax? Float sixty-four tops out near e to the seven hundred and nine. Scores of a thousand, a thousand and one, and a thousand and two overflow to infinity, and infinity over infinity is not a number, three times.

q7-fix.text: Softmax doesn't change when every score shifts by the same amount. Subtract the largest, and the biggest exponent is zero: nine, twenty-four and sixty-seven percent.

q7-log.text: One step further: the loss takes a log. Give the right class a score of a hundred against a thousand, and its probability underflows to zero, whose log is minus infinity. Log-softmax computes minus nine hundred directly, so a loss should take the raw scores.

q8.text: Question eight. How do you implement mini-batching for training? Shuffle the row indices once per epoch, slice them in fixed steps, and index features and labels with the same slice. Ten rows in batches of four give four, four and two. The last batch is short, and that's fine.

q8-seed.text: But don't reseed on every call. A generator that seeds itself the same way each time deals every epoch in the same order. Pass one random generator through the whole run, and each epoch gets a new order.

q9.text: Question nine. How do you shuffle features and labels together correctly? One permutation, applied to both. Shuffle them separately, and every row gets another row's label. On the breast cancer data, logistic regression drops from ninety-six percent to fifty-three percent, worse than always guessing benign, at sixty-three.

q10.text: Question ten. What is reservoir sampling, and when is it useful? It keeps a uniform sample of k items from a stream of unknown length, in one pass, with memory for k. Keep the first k. After that, item number i replaces a random slot with probability k over i.

q10-why.text: The follow-up is why that's uniform. Item i gets in with chance k over i. Then each later item, j, knocks it out with chance one over j. Multiply it through, and every item ends at k over n.

q10-sim.text: In a simulation of twenty thousand streams of a thousand log lines, each tenth of the stream supplied ten percent of the sample.

q10-alt.text: The shortcuts fail. The first k lines all come from the start of the day, and keeping each line with probability one percent gives anywhere from five to fifteen, not ten.

r-hash.text: Reach for a hash map for counting, grouping and have-I-seen-this, in constant time on average. Counting labels gives the majority class, the baseline any model has to beat: here, cat, half the time.

r-dedup.text: To deduplicate a list and keep its order, check a set, and append to a list, or use dict from keys, in one line. Both are linear. Sorting first is n log n, and it loses the order.

r-argmax.text: To decode classes from a probability matrix, n rows by k classes, take argmax along axis one: one class per row. Along axis zero you get k answers instead, so check the shape.
r-argmax.spoken: To decode classes from a probability matrix, n rows by k classes, take arg max along axis one: one class per row. Along axis zero you get k answers instead, so check the shape.

r-metrics.text: Accuracy, precision and recall from scratch are boolean masks, summed, with no loop. Handle the empty case: a model that predicts no positives has a precision of zero over zero. NumPy returns not a number; scikit-learn reports zero, with a warning.

r-knn.text: And k-nearest neighbors. The n distances cost n times d. Then a full sort costs n log n, or a heap of size k, n log k. Either way, computing the distances costs more than choosing among them, so repeated queries need an index: a KD-tree, a ball tree, or an approximate one like HNSW.

next.text: Code gives you a number. Statistics says how far to trust it. Next: statistics and probability.

q1-row-rule.text: Put the whole step in one array operation, and keep loops for steps that depend on the step before.

q1-row-ratio.text: Still roughly forty times slower, because the interpreter still runs once per row.
